title: Targeted enzyme discovery using metal-coordination mining.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and opened: Supplementary Data 1-5 archive (36.8 MB compressed; contains SupplementaryDataset2.csv = 946 data rows, 58 columns, 946 unique UniProt protein accessions, 76 network clusters, 844 bacterial / 87 eukaryotic / 1 archaeal); Source Data Fig. 1 spreadsheet (sheet Fig1c = same 946 rows; sheet Fig1d = 215 rows with an 'HXres' column giving the third metal-coordinating residue: D=104, G=93, E=10, '-'=7, A=1); Source Data Extended Data Fig. 10 spreadsheet (2,969 data rows, a 'motif' column with 65 distinct metal-coordination motif strings such as 'HISx2+GLNx1', each class capped at about 71 members); Source Data Fig. 3 spreadsheet (58 rows = roughly 19 substrates x 3 replicates of 'mean % consumption' by the enzyme BtnX). I also checked the Zenodo code record (10.5281/zenodo.19737460, 10.9 MB, code only, CC-BY-4.0) and the GitHub repository file list (demo set of individual PDB structure files). Critically, I tested identifier resolution: of 60 randomly sampled accessions from the Extended Data Fig. 10 table only 23 still return a sequence from current UniProtKB, and of 60 sampled from Supplementary Dataset 2 only 21 do; spot checks (A0A095XKD8, A0A0M3Q111, X7S735) return entryType 'Inactive', reason DELETED 'Not part of a reference proteome'. AlphaFold Protein Structure Database still serves models for those deleted accessions via its per-accession application programming interface.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The pipeline counts: 1.8 million cupin-domain sequences retrieved from InterPro, 530,814 AlphaFold2 models downloaded, 456,585 carrying the canonical two-histidine-plus-aspartate/glutamate iron site, 946 carrying the two-histidine-plus-alanine/glycine site that implies halogenase activity, and 538,160 total two-histidine sites in the cupin fold. Only the 946 figure appears in a file I opened. The enzyme kinetics numbers for AspX and BtnX, the crystal structures (Protein Data Bank entries 9PV1 and 9Q04) and the mutagenesis results were read in the text, not opened.

a1_downloadable.note: No login needed. The Europe PMC bulk supplementary endpoint was too slow to finish, but every file downloaded cleanly from the publisher's open-access content server; I opened them. Licence is CC BY-NC-ND (non-commercial, no derivatives).

a2_label_is_a_column.note: For the headline task (is this cupin-fold enzyme a radical halogenase or not?) the negative class is absent: the 456,585 canonical-site proteins are nowhere in the supplied files, so the label column would have to be built by re-downloading about 530,000 predicted structures and re-running the authors' geometry rule. A motif label IS a column in the Extended Data Fig. 10 table (2,969 rows) and in the Fig. 1d table (215 rows), but those are small, stratified subsamples, not the real dataset.

a3_inputs_present.note: No amino acid sequences and no structures are in any supplied table - only accession codes. Worse, the codes have decayed: roughly 60 percent of sampled accessions are now DELETED from UniProtKB, so sequences must be pulled one at a time from the AlphaFold database or UniParc archive. That is thousands of lookups against a second resource, which is the stated fail condition.

a4_units_stated.note: Not really applicable to the main label, which is a categorical residue motif string. The one quantitative table I opened (Source Data Fig. 3) states its unit explicitly as 'mean % consumption' with standard deviation and replicate number.

a5_enough_rows.note: Largest table with a label column holds 2,969 rows (verified by opening it), spread over 65 classes at about 46-71 rows each. But the biologically measured label - this enzyme really does halogenate - exists for exactly 2 proteins (AspX and BtnX). Passes on the computational label only.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~1.6 GB uncompressed for the whole supplementary archive; ~1.3 MB for the two tables that actually carry labels
a6_fits_laptop.note: The supplied tables are trivially small. Reconstructing the real dataset would mean about 530,000 predicted structures (well over 100 GB), which would fail this check, but that is not required for the subsampled framing.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The 946 putative halogenases in the paper match exactly the 946 rows I counted in SupplementaryDataset2.csv and in the Fig. 1c sheet. Minor mismatch: the paper states a sample size of 3,000 for the Extended Data Fig. 10 network, the file has 2,969 rows. The paper says 70 unexplored clusters plus 6 known families (76) and the file has 76 cluster identifiers - consistent.

a8_label_provenance.note: This is the fatal one, and it fails twice over. (1) Circularity: every label in the dataset is the authors' three-distance geometric rule applied to AlphaFold2-PREDICTED structures, so the label is a downstream product of another model, not a measurement. (2) Leakage by construction: the only available input is the amino acid sequence, and AlphaFold2 is a deterministic function of that sequence, so the label is fully determined by the feature. A sequence-to-motif model would be distilling 'run AlphaFold2, then measure three atom distances' and a near-perfect score would carry no biological information. The genuinely measured functional label (halogenase activity confirmed in vitro) covers 2 proteins out of 946.

existing_models.name: Metal3D / AllMetal3D (three-dimensional convolutional neural networks that predict where a metal ion sits in a protein, and for AllMetal3D also which metal and what geometry)
existing_models.score_and_split: Metal3D reports zinc positions within 0.70 +/- 0.64 Angstrom of the experimental location; split details taken from the search summary, not from re-reading the paper
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved - I only read search-result summaries, so I will not attribute an unsolved-problem statement to them

existing_models.name: MetalNet / MetalNet2 (predicts metal-binding sites across whole proteomes; version 2 encodes residue pairs with ESM-2, a protein language model)
existing_models.score_and_split: MetalNet2 reports F1 of 0.76, recall 0.70, precision 0.83 on a held-out test set drawn from the Protein Data Bank as of May 2023

backbone.name: ESM-2 (a protein language model; the 8-million and 35-million parameter checkpoints run on a laptop processor)
backbone.hardware: 16 GB laptop, processor only, embeddings cached once
backbone.licence: ESM-2 is MIT-licensed; the paper's own data is CC BY-NC-ND, which forbids distributing derived versions

integration.partner_dataset: AlphaFold Protein Structure Database and UniProt/InterPro (would supply the structures and sequences the tables omit)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does a sequence-only model recover the metal-coordination motif that the authors read off predicted structures, cheaply enough to scan the parts of sequence space AlphaFold never modelled? - but this question is unanswerable honestly here because the target is itself an AlphaFold-derived quantity.

controls.positive_control: Would be: recover the 22 proteins annotated in the file as 'Non-haem Fe2+/alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent halogenase' plus the 6 known halogenase families, and separately predict sequence length from sequence as a plumbing check.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the motif labels within cluster and confirm collapse to the per-cluster majority class; ablate the residues near the predicted iron site.
controls.external_validation: Weak. The only independent evidence is 10 experimental Protein Data Bank entries among the 946 rows and 2 enzymes characterised in vitro. No second database, no publication-year column.

honest_claim_h3: A model trained on this data could claim only: 'given an amino acid sequence, I reproduce the metal-coordination motif that a geometric rule assigns to that sequence's AlphaFold2-predicted structure' - not 'I predict whether an enzyme halogenates', because in vitro halogenase activity was measured for 2 of the 946 candidates.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use an enzyme's amino acid sequence to predict which amino acids hold its iron atom, and so whether it halogenates.
plain_idea.train_on: One row per protein: the amino acid sequence (which is NOT in the files and must be fetched per accession) plus taxonomy and protein-family tags. 2,969 rows in the largest labelled table, or 215 rows in the cleanest binary one - both counts verified by opening the files.
plain_idea.predict: The identity of the third amino acid coordinating the iron: an aspartate or glutamate means an ordinary oxygen-adding enzyme, an alanine or glycine leaves a gap for chloride and implies a halogenase. The 'true answer' is not a lab measurement; it is three atom-to-atom distances measured in an AlphaFold2-predicted structure.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Biocatalysis groups who want enzymes that put a chlorine onto an unreactive carbon-hydrogen bond would use a fast sequence-only screen. But because the answer key is computed from the sequence itself, a good score would prove nothing about enzymes.

ml_idea: Freeze ESM-2 embeddings of cupin-superfamily sequences and fit a small classifier head to predict the metal-coordination motif (halogenase-type two-histidine-plus-alanine/glycine versus canonical two-histidine-plus-aspartate/glutamate), held out by sequence-identity cluster. Rejected because the target is a deterministic function of the input routed through AlphaFold2.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed. About 3,000 sequences at roughly 1-2 per second on a laptop processor with the 35-million-parameter ESM-2 checkpoint gives under an hour of embedding; a logistic-regression head over 3,000 rows is seconds. The real cost is the 3,000 individual AlphaFold-database or UniParc lookups needed to obtain sequences at all, since about 60 percent of the accessions are deleted from UniProtKB.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Ask where the label came from before downloading anything: it is a geometric rule applied to AlphaFold2 predictions, so it is computable from the sequence you would use as input. Second cheapest: count rows with a measured halogenation assay - the answer is 2.

verdict_reason: Fails Part A on three counts, decisively on A8 (label provenance). Every label in this paper's tables is the authors' three-distance geometric rule applied to AlphaFold2-predicted structures, and AlphaFold2 is a deterministic function of the amino acid sequence that would be the model's only input - so the target is computable from the features through an intermediate model. A near-perfect score would mean the model learned to imitate AlphaFold plus a ruler, not biology. A2 also fails because the negative class (456,585 canonical-site proteins) is in no supplied file and would have to be rebuilt from roughly 530,000 structure downloads, and A3 fails because no sequences are present and about 60 percent of the accessions are now DELETED from UniProtKB (verified by sampling 120 accessions). The genuinely measured label - confirmed halogenase activity - exists for 2 proteins. The paper is a strong piece of science and the 946-protein atlas is a real community resource; it is just not a supervised-learning dataset. Salvageable fragment, noted for completeness: the 946-row table carries UniParc identifiers for all rows, so it would make a clean positive set for an unsupervised or retrieval-style study, and the finding that most of its accessions have been deleted from UniProtKB is itself worth a short note.
